profile.purpose: Shows how to sharpen a hard-steel Japanese-style knife on water stones, with knife maker Barney, and covers related knife care.
profile.thesis: Whetstones are presented as the best way to sharpen a knife because they give control over how much metal is removed, and the video walks through the setup, angle, stroke technique, grit progression, stropping and care for hard-steel knives.
key_takeaways: Contrasts manual and electric sharpeners with water stones, which give more control and remove less metal.
Explains the differences between softer Western steel and harder Japanese or high-carbon steel in edge retention and ease of sharpening.
Water stones are soaked before use, kept lubricated, set in a tray on a towel, and flattened with a stone fixer that also raises a sharpening slurry.
Gives a trigonometry shortcut for setting the angle: lift the spine by a quarter of the blade width for about 15 degrees, or a third for about 20 degrees.

Stroke method: heel at the top of the stone, use the full stone and blade length, lighter pressure pushing and more pulling, then 16-20 strokes per side followed by fewer and fewer alternating strokes.
Covers grit numbers (300, 800, 1200, 2000, 6000 and up) and which ones most people need, and recommends single-grit King stones.
Advises against honing rods on hard steel knives and suggests a leather strop with compound, pulling strokes only.
Includes a tomato slicing test, plus tips on how often to sharpen and how to store knives.

outline.title: Intro and why use whetstones
outline.summary: Kenji introduces Barney of Kan knives and explains why he prefers whetstones over manual or electric sharpeners.

outline.title: Hard vs soft steel
outline.summary: Barney and Kenji compare softer Western European steel with harder Japanese and high-carbon steel, covering edge retention, care and how hard each is to sharpen.

outline.title: Water stones, grits and setup
outline.summary: Explains soaking water stones, grit numbers, the tray-and-towel setup, and flattening the stone with a stone fixer, which also creates the sharpening slurry.

outline.title: Bevels and setting the angle
outline.summary: Covers single and double bevel knives, typical 15 and 20 degree angles, and a trigonometry trick for estimating the angle by eye.

outline.title: Sharpening stroke technique
outline.summary: Shows starting with the heel at the top of the stone, hand placement and pressure, keeping the stone wet, and the decreasing stroke-count pattern for an even edge.

outline.title: How often to sharpen and avoiding damage
outline.summary: Kenji explains rotating through his knives and sharpening a few times a year, and lists ways to protect an edge: cutting boards only, no bones, frozen food or glass.

outline.title: Grit progression and stone recommendations
outline.summary: Discusses which grits to progress through, when very fine grits are worth it, and why single-grit King stones beat small cheap double-sided ones.

outline.title: Honing rods vs strops
outline.summary: Explains why honing rods can chip hard steel knives and demonstrates a leather strop with green compound, using pulling strokes only.

outline.title: Sharpness test and storage
outline.summary: Covers why a sharp knife is safer, a tomato slicing test with the resharpened knife and a new Kan knife, and advice on storing knives in a block or edge guard.

After listing 800, 1200, 2000 and 6000, he revises it: he would probably just go from 800 to 2000 and might finish there.
